articles.title: As drug prices in Europe soar, Public Pharma advocates are charting a new course
articles.author: Peoples Health Dispatch
articles.content: Health workers, activists, and access to medicines advocates have gathered in Frankfurt on October 22-23 for the 2nd Public Pharma Conference . The event builds on roughly two years of work by the Public Pharma for Europe Coalition , which aims to construct an alternative vision for the region’s pharmaceutical landscape – and to strengthen the links needed to turn that vision into reality. “When we had the first conference in 2024, we realized there are many people practically working on this topic who shared a similar vision and a similar goal,” Frauke Heller from medico international told BreakThrough News . The new conference aims to open the space to even more advocates, she added, in a region where the Big Pharma lobby remains extremely influential. Read more: Public pharma infrastructure could give the world access to a treasure trove of medicines The first day focused on the coalition’s expansion and the shifting global landscape it faces, including growing concerns about the availability and affordability of medicines across Europe. Speakers – including commons activist Gaëlle Krikorian, Tim Joye, president of Medics for the People (MPLP-GVHV), researcher Tineke Kleinhoudt-Vliek, and Jan Wintgens, coordinator of the People’s Health Movement (PHM) Public Pharma program in Europe – detailed how a system reliant on Big Pharma is deepening these access problems. Their interventions also highlighted that alternatives already exist. Kleinhoudt-Vliek pointed to dozens of existing examples of drug research, development, and innovation projects in Europe alone that are supported by the public sector in different ways. “This used to happen only in ‘market-failure’ areas, but it’s now moving into profitable drugs too,” she pointed out. Austerity is exacerbating access to medicines issues The conference recognized that rising drug prices in Europe have sharpened the visibility of this issue compared to earlier years, when social security systems were still able to secure access to medicines for patients in the region. That is less the case today, as Big Pharma companies set exorbitant prices for new products – and social security systems themselves are undermined by austerity. The effects are felt across the region, with Joye and Krikorian turning to examples from Belgium and France. In Belgium, Joye said, the case of a family forced to fundraise close to €2 million for a spinal muscular atrophy injection for a baby reinforced MPLP’s efforts to envision a different pharma system. In France, current drug prices have been driving both patients and pharmacists “out of their minds,” Krikorian emphasized, prompting them to become more critical of the whole system. Read more: Listening through the social stethoscope: MPLP’s health workers redefine care in Belgium These developments cannot be separated from the situation affecting the world today, related to the weakening position of the United States, speakers and participants seemed to agree. “If we compare the world in March 2024 to today, the difference is enormous,” Joye said, citing a recent decision by drug giant GSK to cut 1,200 jobs from its 8,000-strong operations in Belgium. “This is not a company in financial difficulties: they’re cutting jobs because they’re planning to shift part of their operations to the US under the influence of the Trump administration.” People in Europe are growing increasingly scared of war, due to their governments’ arms race, he added, but also of losing their jobs. “Politicians using this fear to increase the power of the multinationals instead of changing the system.” Experiences from socialism and the Global South As the European Public Pharma coalition continues to grow its ranks, it remains attentive to experiences from the past, including the public production of vaccines in formerly socialist states of Eastern Europe – as presented by David Franco from Public Pharma for Europe and Goran Jeras from the Cooperative for Ethical Financing. The 2nd Public Pharma Conference brought together dozens of activists from around Europe. Source: Sofie Blancke/MPLP-GVHV But the platform is also looking toward practical examples of orienting pharmaceutical research and production away from a profit-making model. This includes the work of Cuban scientists, who have achieved groundbreaking breakthroughs despite the ongoing blockade imposed by the US, as well as medical research institutes in Brazil and efforts to establish public production of therapies in Canada. Gerardo Guillén from the China-Cuba Biotechnology Innovation Center linked the island’s breakthroughs – including interferon therapy , innovative treatments for diabetic foot , and COVID-19 medicines – to the people-centered healthcare erected following the revolution. Cuba’s persistent research and innovation cannot be separated from Fidel Castro ‘s appeal for a science-based revolution – a science that serves the needs of the people – Guillén pointed out. Read more: Humanity owes Cuba: unilateral coercive measures and the politics of punishment Another example came from Martin Häuer of the Open Source Imaging Initiative (OSI²), who walked participants through existing efforts to build MR imaging machines using open-source tools. For now, the project team was able to assemble functioning prototypes for around €20,000 – with reassembly in low-income health systems like Ghana’s projected at around €24,000. This amount represents roughly 10% of the standard market price of an MRI: significantly increasing the chance of the technology becoming more widely accessible and showing how significant the impact of these initiatives can be globally. People’s Health Dispatch is a monthly bulletin published by the People’s Health Movement and Peoples Dispatch . For more articles and to subscribe to People’s Health Dispatch, click here.

articles.title: Luisa González, former presidential candidate and opposition leader, is arrested in Ecuador
articles.author: BreakThrough News
articles.content: Former President Rafael Correa (2007–2017) posted on X in the early hours of the morning in Ecuador that Luisa González, a two-time presidential candidate (2023 and 2025) for the Citizen Revolution (RC) party, had been arrested. “They arrested Luisa González. ENOUGH IS ENOUGH!” wrote the former progressive leader. The National Police confirmed this to the media outlet PRIMICIAS . González was reportedly arrested on suspicion of money laundering. The National Prosecutor’s Office also confirmed this, reporting that the arrest is related to alleged irregularities in political financing and campaign spending in 2023. González, who advanced to the runoff in both elections and lost both times to the current president, right-wing candidate Daniel Noboa, has repeatedly claimed that the legal proceedings against her are part of a broader campaign of political persecution targeting anyone who criticizes the current government. A few hours after his arrest, González wrote on X : “We have reached an untenable situation. Noboa’s dictatorship has not only led our beloved country into economic disaster, with rampant violence and corruption, but attacks on civil liberties and political persecution are a constant reality. The dictatorship’s political prisoners are being mistreated and tortured.” She added : “Today it is my turn to be arrested on an absurd charge. I will respond with the dignity of Ecuadorians who owe nothing and who are committed to securing Ecuador’s freedom and a better future for the country.” A flood of legal proceedings against González In January 2026, the prosecutor’s office and the police raided Luisa González’s home as part of the case known as “Caja Chica,” which was investigating an alleged money laundering offense. The prosecutor’s office claimed there was evidence of money flowing in from Venezuela to fund González’s 2023 election campaign. In August, González said she had been notified of a preliminary investigation into the alleged crime of demanding acts that entail receiving undue benefits. In September, González was again notified by the Prosecutor’s Office of her inclusion in a preliminary investigation into an alleged crime of failure to report a crime due to her profession, position, or occupation – that is, for allegedly failing to report a crime in the course of her professional duties. In all three cases, the former presidential candidate and leader of the largest opposition party has denounced these actions as political persecution carried out through the judicial system: “The harassment and persecution don’t stop, but neither does my hope for a better country. Giving up is not an option.” Political persecution or enforcement of the law? In addition, González, who intended to run for the office of prefect of Manabí in the upcoming regional elections in November, was unable to register her candidacy due to a refusal by the electoral oversight bodies, citing alleged mismanagement of administrative matters. The RC once again denounced this obstacle as part of a broader campaign of political persecution aimed at preventing opposition candidates who might win their positions in the elections from participating, whether through administrative sanctions or criminal proceedings. Thus, according to these allegations, the government has managed to co-opt several oversight institutions with the power to impose sanctions—such as the prosecutor’s office and the electoral courts – and is using them to persecute and prevent the participation of opposition politicians who have a chance of challenging the executive branch for power. For his part, Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa has repeatedly denied that his administration has been behind the accusations, sanctions, and arrests targeting his opponents, and he asserted that these are proceedings carried out by institutions independent of his government. “We do not target individuals; we have no interest in targeting individuals – we pursue criminals. There is no political persecution of any kind here,” the Ecuadorian president said in early 2026. Despite these statements, the opposition remains steadfast in its accusations against the Ecuadorian president, especially following cases in which mayors of the country’s largest cities – Guayaquil, Cuenca, and Quito, the capital – have faced imprisonment, criminal proceedings, and ongoing judicial investigations. The most notorious case in Ecuador involves the mayor of Guayaquil (the country’s most populous city), opposition figure Aquiles Álvarez, who was arrested and imprisoned in a maximum-security prison several months ago on charges of illegal hydrocarbon trafficking and organized crime. Similarly, in June 2026, the then-mayor of Cuenca, Cristian Zamora (also a member of the opposition) was suspended by the Contentious-Electoral Court over an alleged case of political violence. For its part, the prosecutor’s office requested that charges be filed against him in September of that same year for an alleged crime of illicit enrichment. And while there are other high-profile cases in Ecuador, the RC has stated that there is a concerted effort to prevent the current mayor of Quito, Pabel Muñoz (who is seeking reelection) from participating in the electoral process at all costs. Muñoz has so far managed to evade the sanctions and constant accusations against him, but on October 21, the prosecutor’s office and the police raided the mayor’s offices as part of an investigation into an alleged embezzlement offense. This has led several politicians to believe that the raid is a new ploy to prevent Muñoz—who leads in the polls – from participating in the elections and, even more so, to imprison him, as was done with his party colleague, Aquiles Álvarez. This is what the Prefect of Pichincha, Paola Pabón, said : “People’s lives do not improve by imprisoning opponents; citizens’ circumstances change for the better when there is a political class committed to the common good.”

articles.title: Mehdi Hasan on AIPAC’s Role in El-Sayed vs. Rogers Race in Michigan & Trump’s Targeting of Ilhan Omar
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : We are less than two weeks away from the November 3rd midterm elections that’ll determine control of Congress. To win the Senate, Democrats need to flip four Republican seats and hold three of their own, including Michigan, one of the most closely watched races. Democrat Dr. Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers are in a tight race for an open seat. El-Sayed is a former public health official who’s campaigning on a platform of Medicare for All, ending military aid to Israel, and getting corporate money out of politics. Rogers is a former Republican congressmember backed by President Trump. On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that AIPAC , the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, has plans to quietly give up to $9 million to a super PAC supporting Mike Rogers. The money started being given after October 14th, which meant the money will not need to be disclosed until after the election. On Wednesday, the Senate candidates in Michigan met in their final debate. Dr. El-Sayed criticized Rogers’ connection to AIPAC and his support for the war on Iran. DR. ABDUL EL- SAYED : He’s still cheerleading the war that you are paying for, a war we never should have fought in the first place. You send this man to the U.S. Senate, do not be surprised when we fight more wars, we accrue more national debt, and he does not stand up for you for the price of your gas or the price of your groceries. Why? He’s bought off by the same weapons manufacturers. AIPAC , we just heard, is going to put, what, $9 million into his campaign in the next two weeks alone? Well, that’s what you get when you have an AIPAC -backed politician. NERMEEN SHAIKH : The New York Times broke the news about AIPAC’s plans to spend $9 million to help Rogers on the same day that AIPAC announced that it will stop endorsing candidates or making direct contributions through its PAC , but it confirmed it will continue influencing elections through its super PAC , United Democracy Project, and other fundraising tools. During the Democratic primary, AIPAC’s super PAC spent more than $30 million in an unsuccessful effort to defeat El-Sayed. The New York Times reports AIPAC decided to spend heavily to help Mike Rogers, after he welcomed AIPAC’s support when asked this question by the moderator during their first debate. RICK ALBIN : Congressman Rogers, Axios reported that your allies asked AIPAC not to advertise on your behalf, and Axios also reported that you talked with the chair of AIPAC , and the next day they discontinued an ad on your behalf. Do you welcome AIPAC’s public support, given that you do support many pro-Israeli positions? You have 60 seconds. MIKE ROGERS : Anybody that wants to help my campaign stop a guy who can’t condemn terrorism in our own country because he’s so close to the people who are supporting the Muslim Brotherhood — DR. ABDUL EL- SAYED : Again, I’ve condemned them. MIKE ROGERS : — you bet, I’ll take all of that help. AMY GOODMAN : During Wednesday’s debate in Michigan, Republican Mike Rogers again claimed, without evidence, that Abdul El-Sayed had ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. Dr. El-Sayed has repeatedly denied the claim and denounced the accusation as Islamophobic. If elected, El-Sayed would become the first Muslim to serve in the U.S. Senate. During last night’s debate, he responded to Rogers’ attack. DR. ABDUL EL- SAYED : He keeps raising this question about this association with an organization I’ve never been a part of, because my mom, who’s a nurse in Missouri? It doesn’t make any sense, and it’s actually really quite beneath you, Mike. It’s really quite beneath you. … I am proud of America. I’m proud to be an American. I’m proud of our Constitution, that guarantees all of us the right to pray as we choose to pray. AMY GOODMAN : We’re joined right now by Mehdi Hasan, editor-in-chief and CEO of Zeteo, also the executive producer of the new Zeteo documentary Night Flower: Inside AIPAC’s Fight for Influence . We’ll talk more about the documentary in a minute, but, Mehdi, I want to begin in Michigan. You just heard the lede. We’re less than two weeks away from the midterm elections. AIPAC spent over $30 million in an attempt to defeat El-Sayed in the primary. They didn’t succeed. If you can talk about the latest news out of Michigan and the significance of this race for the country and the attacks on El-Sayed by his opponent? MEHDI HASAN : Thank you, Amy. A massively significant race, consequential for both sides. Both sides have a lot riding on this race, because if Abdul El-Sayed wins, it will be a reminder that the left can win in a swing state like Michigan, not just in a blue city like New York City or a blue district in Colorado or whatever it is. And it will be actually a moment to say, “You know what? Americans rejected Islamophobia,” brazen Islamophobia, from the president of the United States downwards, who refuses to call Abdul El-Sayed by his name, calls him a jihadist. So, it’s a major moment, I think, if he wins, especially going up against AIPAC money. He’ll be going up against AIPAC money, the president of the United States, unconstrained Islamophobia and members of his own party. I mean, the former chair of the Michigan Democratic Party is not voting for him. So, there’s a real — there’s a real challenge here for the left, in particular, and for people of Muslim faith in this country, that this race means a lot. And, of course, for the Democratic Party, they really need Michigan, ideally, to take back the Senate. And then, of course, for Republicans, it’s a major move, because, you know, Donald Trump is already dragging down all their candidates. Mike Rogers was pretending to be this moderate candidate in Michigan, and he can’t seem to seal the deal a second time round. He lost to Elissa Slotkin narrowly in 2024, and now he’s trying again. But his campaign is nothing but bigotry. So, it’s a really existential moment. If Abdul El-Sayed loses, by the way, people in the Democratic Party — forget the Republicans — people in the Democratic Party will say, Amy, “Look, we tried the left’s way. We tried a candidate who supports Medicare for All. We tried a candidate who opposes arms to Israel. We tried a diverse Muslim candidate. Didn’t work. We’re not going to do that again.” So, there’s a lot riding on this race. NERMEEN SHAIKH : Mehdi, could you also explain this super PAC , United — MEHDI HASAN : Yeah. NERMEEN SHAIKH : — Democracy Project, and what role it’s been playing so far in these weeks leading up to the midterms? MEHDI HASAN : So, the UDP , the United Democracy Project, is AIPAC’s super PAC . And just to be clear to people, historically, AIPAC didn’t have a super PAC . They only brought this up a few years ago to directly inject dark money into campaigns like Haley Stevens’s primary campaign against Abdul El-Sayed, where they spent around $30 million. Over the course of this cycle, I believe the UDP has spent anywhere between $80 million and $100 million, is my understanding. It’s one of the big spending super PACs by issue. What’s interesting about the United Democracy Project is twofold. Number one, it’s funded by a lot of Republican billionaires. So, when it interferes in Democratic primaries, when it backs Democratic candidates, moderate types against leftists, that’s Republican money injected into a Democratic primary. It’s why Bernie Sanders, among others, has said the Democratic Party should ban AIPAC from taking — you know, ban candidates from taking money from AIPAC in Democratic primaries. The other really interesting point about the United Democracy Project, and this is why we made the film about AIPAC , is AIPAC is super unpopular. It’s super toxic. Israel is super unpopular, super toxic in American political discourse for the first time. And so, when you watch United Democracy Project attack ads, Nermeen, they don’t mention Israel. They will attack a candidate like Abdul El-Sayed. They’ll say, “Oh, he’s not loyal to the Democratic Party,” or he’s this, or he’s that. They don’t actually mention Israel. What have you got to hide? Why wouldn’t you mention Israel? Because they don’t even run on their own issue. They keep that quiet, because they operate in the dark. They operate in the shadows, which is why we called our film Night Flower . AMY GOODMAN : And we’re going to talk about that film in just a minute, Mehdi, but I want to ask about the Trump administration’s targeting of Democratic Congressmember Ilhan Omar. MEHDI HASAN : Oh, yeah. AMY GOODMAN : On Tuesday, Trump told reporters that Omar could go to jail. His comments come days after Homeland Security federal agents raided her home in D.C. as part of Trump’s efforts to strip Omar of U.S. citizenship and deport her. She came here as a child. The Trump administration has claimed, without evidence, she committed immigration fraud in her naturalization process. MEHDI HASAN : Yeah. AMY GOODMAN : This is President Trump. PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP : Well, she could be. She could also go to jail. She could also go to jail. You know, they keep talking about deportation. No, she could go to jail. This is just my opinion. I think she’s a sick and very dishonest person, but — who hates our country. And she comes from a country that is essentially not even a country, Somalia. It’s a real [bleep]house. AMY GOODMAN : He originally said that he had nothing to do with the raid on her home. MEHDI HASAN : Yeah. AMY GOODMAN : But if you can talk about the significance — MEHDI HASAN : Yes. AMY GOODMAN : — of this moment? MEHDI HASAN : So, before I get into the Ilhan Omar raid, notice what he said there at the end. He said it’s effectively not a country, Somalia. He’s been on racist diatribes against Somalia for many months now, calling Somalis “low-IQ,” calling Somalis “garbage” and “crooks,” just basically neo-Nazi rhetoric. And I would note that our media goes crazy if you question Israel’s right to exist, and yet the president of the United States says an entire African country doesn’t exist as a country. No outrage from our media. I just want to put that out there. In terms of the Ilhan Omar raid and Donald Trump, Donald Trump has only two skills in life, Amy, only two things he does well. Number one, he’s an authoritarian. He knows how to be authoritarian. He’s a wannabe dictator. And therefore, when he goes after his enemies — he warned people. He said, “I will be vengeant. I will take retribution.” And he’s doing it. It’s one of the few campaign pledges he’s keeping to. He’s gone after many of his opponents. He arrested Don Lemon. He’s targeted people like Tish James. And now he’s raided the home, via his DHS , of Ilhan Omar, who he’s been obsessed with for many, many years — a clearly authoritarian move. Immigration fraud, what a load of nonsense. There’s reporting that the Trump administration, in term one, looked into Ilhan Omar’s naturalization as a teenager and couldn’t find any evidence against her. So this is purely a fishing expedition. This is purely what even the right-wing media is calling “dumpster diving,” looking for stuff they can try and pin on her. And, of course, it’s intimidation: “Watch out! This is what the federal government can do to a member of Congress.” That’s number one, authoritarianism. And number two, what he’s great at is accusing everyone else of what he’s guilty of. Right? So, when he says, “Oh, she’s going to go to prison,” well, actually, the person who should have gone to prison is the man who was convicted of multiple felonies, Donald J. Trump, in New York City; the man who was indicted for multiple felonies in multiple states, which conveniently went away when he ran for president and was elected president; the man who was found liable for sexual abuse in a civil trial in New York. You know, this man is a criminal, and yet he’s accusing everyone else of being a criminal. As for immigration fraud, Elon Musk’s brother — the top donor to the Republican Party in this cycle — is on record, on video, saying, “My brother and I came here as illegal immigrants.” Right? That’s what Elon Musk’s brother Kimbal has said on tape. Melania Trump, in 2016, was asked how she got her Einstein visa, and did she work on a visa she wasn’t supposed to work on before she got that Einstein visa. She said she would give us a press conference to clarify her immigration status in two weeks. Amy, it’s been 10 years. No sign of that press conference. Page 2 The growing controversy over AIPAC’s impact on U.S. politics is the subject of a new Zeteo documentary titled Night Flower: Inside AIPAC’s Fight for Influence . The film examines AIPAC’s history and its role in shaping U.S. policy toward Israel, and questions whether its activities warrant further scrutiny under the Foreign Agents Registration Act, or FARA . “It says that you have to register under this law if you are acting at the request of a foreign government,” says Dion Nissenbaum, the filmmaker behind Night Flower: Inside AIPAC’s Fight for Influence . “And we talked to numerous people who showed us several examples of how AIPAC is acting at the request of Israel.” Referencing the title of the film, Night Flower , Zeteo editor-in-chief Mehdi Hasan says AIPAC “blossoms in the dark, shrivels in the light. We’re trying to put some sunlight onto AIPAC .” Page 3 A court in India on Wednesday ordered the release of two leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party, the youth-led movement that has led historic waves of protests in India since the summer. Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were detained amid massive protests last week after they scaled a barricade to enter a site popular for protest, unfurled the national flag and called for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Kumar oversaw the deletion of 130 million names from the voter rolls in India since June of last year. Opposition parties say those impacted are primarily Muslims and other minorities less likely to support the BJP , the Hindu nationalist ruling party of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. “You have a deep and wide — an ideologically wide — historical culture of resistance in India,” says acclaimed writer and activist Arundhati Roy. At the same time, the Modi government “has three things in its playbook: One is false-flag attacks, two is engineering communal riots, and the third is massive repression. And I don’t think we’ve seen its hand yet.”

articles.content: A court in India on Wednesday ordered the release of two leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party, the youth-led movement that has led historic waves of protests in India since the summer. Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were detained amid massive protests last week after they scaled a barricade to enter a site popular for protest, unfurled the national flag and called for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Kumar oversaw the deletion of 130 million names from the voter rolls in India since June of last year. Opposition parties say those impacted are primarily Muslims and other minorities less likely to support the BJP , the Hindu nationalist ruling party of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. “You have a deep and wide — an ideologically wide — historical culture of resistance in India,” says acclaimed writer and activist Arundhati Roy. At the same time, the Modi government “has three things in its playbook: One is false-flag attacks, two is engineering communal riots, and the third is massive repression. And I don’t think we’ve seen its hand yet.”

articles.title: Drone strikes kill hundreds in just days in Sudan
articles.author: Pavan Kulkarni
articles.content: Drone strikes in war-torn Sudan have killed hundreds in just three days. Most of the deaths were in West Kordofan state, including in an area contested with South Sudan, sparking fears of a spillover of the war. The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) reportedly killed 41 people by striking a gathering of Internally Displaced People (IDPs) near Sudan’s southeastern border with Ethiopia in the Blue Nile state last Friday, October 9. Later on Sunday, October 18, air defenses of the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), which heads the government, intercepted multiple suicide drones launched by the RSF. The drones targeted Upper Atbara and Setit dam complex in Gedaref state, and the Khashm El-Girba dam in neighboring Kassala. The following day, on October 19, the RSF launched a wave of drones toward the airport in the national capital, Khartoum. While the air defenses intercepted most of them, one drone struck near the airport, killing four people, including three children . The RSF took over the capital soon after starting this war in April 2023 against the SAF, the national army with which it had ruled as part of a military junta. The SAF regained control of the capital in March 2025. In the meantime, later in October 2025, the RSF consolidated control over most of Sudan’s vast western region of Darfur, overrunning the SAF’s last holdout, El Fasher , and depopulating the city in a campaign deemed genocidal by a UN investigation. Read more: A bloodbath visible from space: RSF’s massacres in Sudan’s El Fasher After thus taking over Darfur – except for some SAF small holdouts on the border with Chad – the RSF has since been pushing eastward toward Khartoum. The Kordofan region in between, comprising three states, has since become a main front of this war. Here, on October 18, in West Kordofan’s RSF-controlled town of al-Dabba, SAF struck a transport hub that was crowded on a market day, killing 80 people on the spot. 30 others later died in hospital. Another SAF drone also struck a market in the Al-Mujlad town. Then, on the morning of October 19, SAF drones struck yet another market it suspected to be a source of fuel supply for the RSF, killing 153 people in Abyei, an area disputed by Sudan and South Sudan, ever since the latter seceded from the former in 2011.​ This area in the Nile oil basin has over 4,000 UN peacekeepers and is jointly administered by Sudan and South Sudan. South Sudan’s government summoned Sudan’s ambassador to protest this strike. A spillover of Sudan’s war into South Sudan could have dire consequences, especially since South Sudan, the world’s youngest country, is itself at a heightened risk of slipping back into its own disastrous civil war, which had claimed up to 400,000 lives between late 2013 and mid-2015.​ The death count of the war in Sudan has been lost after exceeding 150,000 as early as June 2024 . By the time the war entered its fourth year in April 2026, drone strikes had become the main driver of civilian casualties in this war, causing 80% of all the civilian deaths in the first four months of this year, killing at least 880 people. “We are alarmed by the continued deadly drone strikes across the country that are killing civilians, including children, and that are disrupting essential services,” UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said on October 19. ​Read more: The war in Sudan is “between two wings of a comprador parasitic capitalist class”

articles.title: We beat the Trump administration in court. Now we’re going to the ICC to hold the U.S. accountable for the Gaza genocide
articles.author: Tariq Ra’ouf
articles.content: A recent lawsuit successfully challenged the Trump administration's assault on the International Criminal Court. Now, families like mine, whose relatives have been killed with U.S.-supplied weapons in Gaza, might finally have a chance at justice.

articles.title: Trump is sunk
articles.author: Tempest National Committee
articles.content: T o put it mildly, Trump is not having a good day. He is facing challenges from above: The Federal Reserve increased interest rates against his wishes. The Supreme Court ruled against his attempt to limit voting by mail. Judges have thwarted him on such issues as the Kennedy Center and his attempt to ban news outlets from the White House. Previously loyal Republicans are fleeing now that a Trump endorsement has become a curse . Major far-right media figures such as Tucker Carlson, Marjorie Taylor Greene and Joe Rogan have broken with him. Impeachment and corruption charges are looming. In addition, he is facing discontent from below: His approval ratings are at record lows . According to polls, 65 percent of voters disapprove of Trump, more than twice as many as the 32 percent who approve. His policies are even more unpopular than they have always been, with just 17 percent approving of his handling of the economy. Increasingly, Trump is seen as self-serving and corrupt, no longer the “outsider” alternative to elite politics. As one Republican pollster puts it, in a guest essay called “ The Trump Brand Has Tanked ”: “Voters don’t think the economy is working for them, and they think it’s being rigged more and more in favor of a precious few who are cozied up to our nation’s leaders.” Everyone is asking, “Why is this happening now?” While the answers vary, the universally acknowledged truth is that the war in Iran is the number one culprit, particularly because it is worsening the ongoing affordability crisis. The economic fallout from the war is impacting everyone through soaring fuel prices and higher costs of living domestically. This impact is on top of the generalized instability and suffering the war has provoked globally. The U.S. economy has continued to grow because of enormous investment in artificial intelligence, but this has raised fears of a massive crash if and when the AI bubble bursts. Trump, of course, ran on the promise of ending deeply unpopular “forever wars,” so his exploits abroad are seen as a betrayal by some of his base. And significantly, sections of that base are turning against him. In a New York Times opinion piece called “Trump’s Luck is Finally Running Out,” Thomas Edsall quotes Charlie Cook: “Over the last 90 days, President Trump’s political standing has transitioned from very unpopular to toxic and now to radioactive.” Edsall shares this account from Amy Walter of The Cook Report: Trump’s staying power in our politics — even, astonishingly, despite the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol — gave the president the confidence and latitude to pursue unpopular policies and blow off scandals that would have sunk any of his predecessors. But now, the economic consequences of his sweeping tariffs and the war in Iran have done the one thing all the controversies of his first term were never able to do: splinter his coalition and sink his approval ratings to all-time lows. It is certainly gratifying to see the unbearably arrogant and smug Trump brought down. But this isn’t a moment that we can celebrate. As The Guardian put it in September, “The weaker he gets, the more dangerous he gets: Trump lashes out as his power wanes.” Trump’s relative weakness has not slowed the ruthless tide of xenophobic, racist, and transphobic scapegoating and attacks. Mass detentions and deportations continue . The recent ICE raid on the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar is a chilling example of how far the forces of reaction are willing to go. Trump’s fear of losing the elections has led him to extreme attempts to undermine liberal democracy, something that is recognized even by conservative critics of the administration such as the neo-conservative Robert Kagan, who says , “We’re heading in the direction of dictatorship.” With varying levels of success, Trump has tried or threatened gerrymandering, restricting mail-in ballots, stationing federal troops or agents at polling stations, and abusing the voter database to throw people off voter lists. Right-wing fear-mongering about hordes of noncitizens voting is, of course, unfounded. Trump recently cited Department of Homeland Security estimates of 16,000 noncitizen residents registered to vote in Nevada. A state investigation brought that number down to 185 and then, after further scrutiny, zero. The Nevada Secretary of State called out such widespread disinformation: DHS officials continue their attempts to intimidate election officials into compliance and deter voters with huge claims of fraud with no evidence…Repeating unsupported claims does not make them true. Given such extreme efforts to prevent people from voting and undermine the elections, we can anticipate more legal and illegal maneuvers in the face of a Trump loss. There will likely be further court challenges. As one commentator writes: The courts have provided mixed verdicts on Mr. Trump’s attempts at vote suppression in advance of the 2026 midterms. But the rulings have handed him an unambiguous gift: a road map for shaping the universe of eligible voters to his liking in the presidential election year of 2028. Democrats are widely predicted to win the elections in November and may even win majorities in both the House and Senate, but they offer no real alternative to the far-right agenda. Where we can make a real difference is in movements, campaigns, strikes and struggles on the streets and in the workplace. Collective organizing from below is the only force that has ever won substantial reforms, no matter who is in office. Many Democrats, including some so-called “progressives,” are bending over backward to distance themselves from issues such as Black Lives Matter, trans rights, and Palestinian rights. If they win the election, it will be a vote against Trump, not a vote for the Democratic Party. In fact, 45 percent of voters say their congressional choice is a vote against Trump , including four out of five Democrats and around half of independents. Charlie Cooke has the perfect metaphor: While many have long predicted that Democrats will enjoy a “blue wave” election, I think of it more as a “red undertow,” which will pull many Republicans under and significantly trim the margins for many others. A blue wave implies an endorsement or affirmation of Democrats and their policies. But the Democrats’ brand is still in tatters. … Fortunately for Democrats, this election will in most cases not be about them. If they do get elected, unless Democrats fight for substantial reforms (which they show no inclination to do), they will only disappoint those with raised expectations and lay the ground for the return of an even more radical GOP in 2028 or 2030, continuing the vicious cycle of the two-party system. Given these realities and the current weakness of movements, it’s understandable that some people are placing their hopes in democratic socialists working within the Democratic Party. A recent message from Alexandria Ocasio Cortez makes the case. Titled “Why I’m feeling hopeful,” it describes her campaigning in upstate NY: Launching this program and speaking with organizers has filled me with hope that the energy to elect Democrats up and down the ballot is out there if we can channel it into turning people out who may have previously felt left behind or that their vote did not matter. The way we do that is by giving people something worth showing up for: Medicare for All, universal childcare, a living wage, and a government that actually works for them. That all sounds wonderful. But it’s not what Democrats of any stripe are delivering anywhere. It is not the agenda of mainstream Democrats. And progressives or democratic socialists who get elected face relentless pressure from the system to toe the line. In the absence of independent mass movements that can act as a counterweight, elected democratic socialists are unable to meet their campaign promises. Rather than pulling the mainstream to the Left, they themselves move to the center and lend weight to mainstream Democrats. Katie Wilson, a democratic socialist who was elected as mayor of Seattle last year, campaigned on promises of taxing the rich and funding housing. Instead, she has delivered a city budget with massive spending cuts, no new taxes, and more money for the cops. In New York City, Zohran Mamdani’s failure to reign in the police has already disappointed and frustrated many of his supporters. The failure is not personal, but systemic: Even the best progressives face the harsh reality of being trapped in a rigged and unbending system once they are elected. This recognition does not mean inaction. Revolutionary socialists don’t abstain from elections. They are an important part of politics that we often will want to participate in, whether around a particular ballot issue or a candidate attached to a movement. But we recognize that elections are the territory of the ruling class, and we will always be weakest there. So, they should never be prioritized. We don’t put them first. It’s a waste of our time and energy. We must not drop our criticisms of mainstream or progressive democrats in office—to do so just leaves the field open to the right wing. We must defend our limited democracy (including civil liberties), but most importantly, we must fight not only for meaningful reforms but also for the transformation of society that will allow genuine and much more expansive democracy. The Democratic Party is not committed to such a transformation, and even if they were, would not have much room to maneuver in the current political system. At an otherwise bleak moment, our reason to be hopeful is that a growing number of people on the Left are dissatisfied with the dominant socialist options, whether reformist or campist . They recognize that we need to build a better alternative. Where we can make a real difference is in movements, campaigns, strikes and struggles on the streets and in the workplace. Collective organizing from below is the only force that has ever won substantial reforms, no matter who is in office. Hundreds of thousands of mostly young people in France, Spain, Belgium and India are currently demonstrating this in mass protests around education, housing and other issues. These are the same forces that have the power to stop the right and revitalize the Left in the U.S. Opinions expressed in signed articles do not necessarily represent the views of the editors or the Tempest Collective. articles.title: Cuba says arrest warrant against Raúl Castro is ‘pathetic Miami circus, with an electoral agenda’
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: Last March, the US justice system reopened a case regarding the alleged responsibility of former Cuban President Raúl Castro in the shooting down of small planes belonging to the organization Brothers to the Rescue in 1996. Cuba has categorically rejected the US accusations. The Caribbean nation argues that the accusation is a distortion of the truth, given that Brothers to the Rescue is considered an organization linked to acts of terrorism and provocation against the country’s government. According to Havana , the aircraft were conducting illegal flights over Cuban airspace. They were reportedly asked repeatedly to refrain from entering Cuban airspace, but these requests were ignored, according to the Cuban justice system. Furthermore, according to the Cuban Foreign Ministry, Havana asked Washington on 25 occasions to prevent these illegal flights. Subsequently, with no response from Washington or Brothers to the Rescue, Cuba proceeded to fire upon the aircraft flying over its territory. However, the US justice system denies Cuba’s version of events and has sought a conviction for these acts. That is how, on October 19, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier succeeded in having his state issue an arrest warrant for Raúl Castro, then Cuba’s Minister of Defense. “Raúl Castro ordered the cold-blooded murder of four Florida residents, and the state will never stop pursuing accountability for that communist conspiracy,” Uthmeier said regarding the arrest warrant. But the Cuban government maintains that Brothers to the Rescue had a different mission than the one it claimed. Cuban Deputy Gerardo Hernández stated : “Although [Brothers to the Rescue] was founded to spot and report the location of rafters to the US Coast Guard in the 1990s, its role shifted toward provocations following the change in immigration policies agreed upon between Washington and Havana in 1995, with the intention of hindering any diplomatic rapprochement and normalization of relations between the two countries.” For his part, Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel condemned the Florida court’s decision: “The reprehensible action taken against the Army General this morning in a pathetic Miami circus, with an electoral agenda, has no legal basis whatsoever – nor will it ever have one – much less a practical one… In the face of every affront, [Raúl Castro] will always find the determination of a people to defend the Revolution.” He added : “That maneuver, cloaked in legal pretense and orchestrated by anti-Cuban politicians against Raúl and against Cuba, deserves our firm condemnation. It is part of their aggressive agenda and a response to their failures in attempting to justify the Embargo and the collective punishment against our people.” For its part, the Mexican government characterized the arrest warrant issued against one of the historic leaders of the 1959 Cuban Revolution as an “electoral maneuver.” This was explained by President Claudia Sheinbaum , who linked the judicial decision to the upcoming midterm elections: “The arrest warrant against Army General Raúl Castro, attributed to the Florida prosecutor’s office, seeks to win the support of segments of the US electorate.” Russia also condemned the arrest warrant against Raúl Castro, calling it “baseless and false,” and linked it to a powerful political group in Florida: “[It is] revenge by the anti-Cuban lobby in Miami,” said the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The decision is part of a series of measures by the Trump administration against the revolutionary government in Havana, which the US president himself has said he would like to see fall and has on some occasions suggested he might launch a military attack on Cuba. Trump has imposed economic and trade sanctions that add to the historic economic and trade embargo the United States has imposed on the island for more than 60 years – an embargo that has caused losses amounting to tens of billions of dollars for a country with a population of just 10 million. Added to this is the recent oil embargo imposed by the United States on the Caribbean island. As a result, throughout 2026, only one oil tanker entered Cuba, which has brought much of the country’s production, transportation, and electricity generation to a standstill. This has led to an increase in mortality rates and reduced access to basic services for the civilian population.

articles.title: Israel deemed main ‘source of insecurity and instability’ in Asia at Baku conference
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: Iran demanded Israel’s expulsion from the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) for its crimes against Palestinians and other countries, calling it “the most important source of insecurity and instability” in the region. “If the international community does not stop America and Israel today, their aggression will spread to all independent countries … it is time for this [Zionist] regime to be expelled from the CICA mechanism,” Iran’s deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said during its meeting on Thursday, October 15. The seventh summit of the 29 member CICA process, formed in 1999 as an inter-governmental forum for establishing peace, security, and stability in Asia was held in Baku, Azerbaijan on Thursday. Prior to Iran putting its demand for Israel’s expulsion, representatives of almost a dozen countries including Iran, Turkiye, Pakistan, Indonesia, Bangladesh, and Egypt walked out of the meeting once the Israeli President Isaac Herzog started speaking. This was the second time this year that a top Israeli official faced mass boycott on international forums. Last month, when Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was addressing the annual session of the UN General Assembly, delegates from 77 countries boycotted his speech over the genocide in Gaza and other wars in the region. Representatives from Kuwait also joined the walk out on Thursday, contradicting recent reports in Israeli and US media about it being one of the probable countries to join the so-called Abraham Accords, devised by US President Donald Trump during his first term in office to end the isolation of Israel in the region. Despite the Trump administration’s push, so far only the UAE, Bahrain, Sudan, and Morocco have joined the accords. Israel is the threat to regional peace Gharibabadi mentioned how Israel has been involved in two illegal wars against his country within 16 months from its continued “occupation of Palestinian territories, violation of the rights of Palestinian people, and the escalation of tensions in Lebanon, Syria, as well as other parts of the region,” the IRNA reported . Gharibabadi claimed that his country believes that “one cannot speak of sustainable security in Asia while remaining indifferent to occupation, aggression, military threats, and violation of the rights of the Palestinian nation.” He also pointed out the broader challenges to regional and global peace and stability, claiming that the CICA meeting was held at a time when the international order is facing “one of its most significant challenges, namely; the “normalization of the use of force, alongside attempts to impose its political will upon independent nations through military aggression, sanctions and threats.” Gharibabadi highlighted the combined role of Israel and the US, claiming each of the Israeli crimes against the Palestinians and other countries in the region is committed with the support provided by the US who acts as a “big brother” to the Zionist regime. Answering the concerns raised by several delegates in the meeting, Gharibabadi underlined that peace in West Asia and safe navigation through the waterways in the region is only possible if there is a permanent end to all kinds of aggression and war and there is respect for its sovereignty and territorial integrity. The CICA conference ended with the adoption of the Baku Declaration , which highlighted the need to address growing military, political, economic, and environmental risks.

articles.title: Russia will not abandon agreements with Iran, Lavrov declares in visit to Tehran
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: During a high-level visit to Tehran earlier this week, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov expressed his country’s official position demanding a restoration of the pre-war situation in the Persian Gulf region and guarantees that there will be no return to war against Iran in the future. Lavrov also claimed that his country was ready to assist in “searching for mutually acceptable solutions to resolve” the “artificial” crisis created by “unprovoked US-Israeli aggression” against Iran. Later on Wednesday, Russian President Vladimir Putin repeated the offer of mediation during the visit of Steve Witkoff, the White House’s special envoy to the Middle East, to Moscow. Lavrov, who visited Iran on Monday, October 18, also reiterated the Russian position that Iran’s responses to US aggression was justified and legitimate and claimed his country has provided whatever political and economic assistance it could to help it face the repercussions of the unlawful US-Israeli war. Lavrov’s statement could be seen as a rebuttal to US President Donald Trump, who appreciated Russia’s supposed neutral role in Iran during the eight-month-long war. Trump claimed it was a “positive” development that Russia did nothing to help and was even “laying off Iran” as the US is hitting Iranians economically and militarily. Trump was forced to withdraw some of its sanctions on Russian energy exports, imposed from 2024, in his bid to secure an energy deal earlier this month. Trump’s move is largely seen as an attempt to lower the impact of the rising gas prices on the prospects of Republican candidates before the upcoming midterm elections. Lavrov, however, cited the Russian veto in the UN against the US attempts to justify its military aggression against Iran, providing humanitarian aid including medicine, other medical supplies and food during the war also claiming that such aid is continued to be “delivered regularly.” Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also appreciated the Russian help during the war and expressed his country’s desire to further deepen cooperation between the two countries. Iran and Russia signed and implemented a 20-year Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty last year. The treaty has provisions of close coordination on issues related to economy, geo-politics, and security. Lavrov pointed out the growing bilateral trade between the two countries in the last two years, despite the war and sanctions they are both facing. According to him, in the first eight months of the present year, the bilateral trade between Russia and Iran grew 10% in comparison to the same period last year. Lavrov also informed that Russian scientists who were withdrawn from Iran’s Bushehr nuclear power plant during the war have started returning gradually. Russia and Iran are closer than ever Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi claimed that bilateral relations and cooperation between Russia and Iran has never been as good as it was today. While addressing a joint press conference with Lavrov in Tehran on Monday, Araghchi reiterated that both the countries maintain close cooperation and consultation on all regional issues, including Iranian relations with the US. He claimed that the two countries agree that the instability and disruption in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz is a result of unprovoked US-Israeli aggression and that they share the vision of a diplomatic solution to all outstanding conflicts. Talking about their mutual understanding about regional issues, such as Lebanon and Palestine, Araghchi claimed that both Russia and Iran agree the “genocide of the Palestinian people and the Israeli regime’s dangerous expansionism in the region must stop.” Lavrov alleged that some countries are trying to push the Palestinian issue to the background, which should not be allowed. He stated that both Iran and Russia would push for the implementation of all relevant UN resolutions because it is “crucial to intensify efforts to resolve the Palestinian issue.” Lavrov also demanded an end to all Israeli hostilities in Lebanon and peace in Yemen, demanding the full implementation of all relevant UN resolutions and previous understandings. Lavrov rejected US threats of secondary sanctions over its relationship with Iran, claiming “despite the challenging situation … Russia has no intention to abandon the implementation of economic and investment agreements with Iran.” As a part of its ongoing war, the Trump administration had announced the complete economic isolation of Iran in August, threatening secondary sanctions against all the countries who still maintained economic relations with it. Only a handful of countries, such as the UAE, have announced compliance with the US attempts to economically isolate Iran so far.
